title: Testing React Components with Testing Library
description: Write behavior-focused component tests, query the UI through accessible roles and names, handle asynchronous updates, and keep test scope aligned with the project's actual runner.
learningOutcomes: Explain the purpose and limits of unit, component, integration, and end-to-end tests.
Test user-visible behavior rather than implementation details or private component state.
Choose Testing Library queries by role, accessible name, label, and intended query semantics.
Use userEvent and async queries to represent real interaction and asynchronous UI updates.
Keep test data, network boundaries, and assertions deterministic.
Write meaningful tests in the project's Vitest + React Testing Library setup and understand what changes if Jest is used.
Control API success and failure behavior with isolated Vitest mocks while asserting user-visible UI outcomes.
Distinguish mock call history, reset behavior, and restoring a spied method in Vitest.
Choose equality assertions based on whether the test requires primitive/value comparison, recursive object equality, or reference identity.
Choose getBy, queryBy and findBy according to immediate presence, expected absence, or asynchronous appearance.
Structure a focused test around Arrange, Act and Assert without treating the pattern as a fixed line-count rule.

blocks.text: Tests give fast feedback about observable behavior

A test encodes an expectation about software behavior. Unit tests isolate a small function, component tests render a UI unit and interact with it, integration tests exercise several collaborating parts, and end-to-end tests cover a full user path in a running application. These categories overlap; the important choice is to test a valuable behavior at the lowest level that can reliably prove it. A large number of brittle tests is not automatically better than a smaller suite that catches meaningful regressions.
Test what a user can observe

React Testing Library encourages tests based on the rendered interface. Prefer assertions such as “the Save button becomes disabled while saving” or “the error is announced” over checking private state variables, internal Hook calls, or a particular component implementation. Tests written around user-visible contracts allow the component to be refactored without rewriting every test, while still catching behavior changes that matter.
Choose a query that matches how the interface is used

items: getByRole is a strong default for interactive controls and landmarks; include the accessible name when it helps identify the intended control.
getByLabelText is useful for form fields with a programmatic label.
getByText can locate visible non-interactive content where no better semantic query expresses the intent.
getBy... queries fail immediately if there are zero or multiple matches, making ambiguity visible.
queryBy... returns null for no match and is useful for asserting that content is absent.
findBy... waits for an element to appear asynchronously and rejects after its timeout if it never appears.

blocks.text: Choose `toBe` or `toEqual` for the intended comparison

In Vitest, `toBe(expected)` uses `Object.is` semantics. It is a good default for primitive values, and it checks reference identity for objects. Two separately created objects can have the same properties but still be different references. `toEqual(expected)` recursively compares object contents, so it is the usual choice when the contract is structural equality. Prefer the matcher that describes the behavior you intend to prove; a passing assertion should explain the requirement, not just make a test green.

steps.title: Create separate but equivalent objects
steps.explanation: `first` and `equivalent` have the same properties, but each object literal creates a different object reference.

steps.title: Assert structural equality and distinct identity
steps.explanation: `toEqual` checks the object contents recursively. `not.toBe` succeeds because the two variables do not point to the same object.

steps.title: Assert that a shared reference is identical
steps.explanation: Assigning `first` to another variable keeps the same reference, so `toBe` succeeds. Choose the matcher based on whether the contract is values or identity.

blocks.prompt: Two separate object literals have the same `id` and `name` properties. Which matcher tests structural equality between them?

options.feedback: Correct. `toEqual` recursively compares object contents, so separate objects with matching property values can satisfy the assertion.
`toBe` uses `Object.is` semantics. For distinct object literals it checks reference identity, so matching properties are not enough.
This checks whether the value is truthy. It does not compare the object's properties with another object.
This matcher is for mock or spy functions and their call history, not for comparing object values.

blocks.explanation: Use `toEqual` for recursive value comparison and `toBe` when reference identity or `Object.is` behavior is the intended contract.

blocks.prompt: After saving, an optional status message should be absent. Which assertion checks for absence without throwing just because the element is missing?

options.feedback: Correct. `queryByRole` returns null when no matching element exists, so it is appropriate for an absence assertion.
`getByRole` throws immediately when there is no match, so the assertion never gets a null value to compare.
`findByRole` returns a promise and waits for an element to appear; it expresses an eventual-presence expectation, not immediate absence.
`getAllByRole` throws when no elements match. Use queryBy when the absence itself is the expected state.

blocks.explanation: Use `queryBy...` to check that an element is absent, `getBy...` for a required immediate match, and `findBy...` when an element should appear asynchronously.

blocks.prompt: What do the three A letters in the AAA test pattern stand for?

options.feedback: Correct. Arrange prepares data/context, Act triggers the behavior, and Assert checks the result.
Async and await may be used in a test, but they are not the AAA test-structure pattern.
These words do not describe the commonly used Arrange, Act, Assert structure.
A test may include analysis and automation, but AAA refers to preparing a scenario, triggering it, then checking the outcome.

blocks.explanation: Arrange the scenario, Act by triggering behavior, and Assert the result. Treat AAA as a readable reasoning structure rather than a requirement for exactly three statements.

blocks.text: Use arrange, act, and assert as a reasoning structure

Arrange prepares data and the test environment, act triggers the behavior, and assert checks the resulting contract. This is a reasoning aid, not a rule that every test must contain exactly three lines. Keep each test focused on one meaningful scenario, use descriptive names, and avoid coupling tests through shared mutable state.
Test asynchronous interfaces deliberately

An interface that fetches data may render loading, success, empty, and error states at different times. Use findBy... for an element that should appear later and waitFor when you need to wait for a specific assertion to become true. Do not use arbitrary sleep timers: they slow the suite and make tests flaky. Mock the network boundary or inject the service so the test controls the response and does not depend on an external API being available.

blocks.text: Control external behavior with Vitest mocks

A mock replaces one dependency boundary with a predictable function, so a test can observe calls and choose a success or failure response without reaching a live API. In this project, use Vitest's `vi.fn()` rather than copying Jest-only setup from the legacy guide. Prefer passing a service into a component or mocking the narrow API boundary; avoid replacing React internals. A mock with no implementation returns `undefined`, so configure its result. `mockResolvedValue` and `mockRejectedValue` represent different promise outcomes. Keep mocks isolated: clearing call history does not necessarily reset the implementation, and global stubs must be restored unless the test configuration does so.

steps.explanation: `mockResolvedValue` makes the returned promise resolve with controlled data. For an error-state test, use a separate mock configured with `mockRejectedValue(new Error(...))`; do not share mutable mock behavior across tests.

blocks.text: Keep mocks isolated between tests

Mocks have call history and behavior. `vi.clearAllMocks()` clears recorded calls but keeps implementations. `vi.resetAllMocks()` clears history and resets mock behavior. `vi.restoreAllMocks()` restores original methods replaced by `vi.spyOn`. A global stub made with `vi.stubGlobal` has separate cleanup through `vi.unstubAllGlobals`. Use the APIs supported by this repository's Vitest version and inspect `vitest.config`; do not assume defaults from another major version or copy Jest-only setup.

steps.title: Restore the real method after the test
steps.explanation: `afterEach` restores spies created with `vi.spyOn`, preventing the replacement from leaking into later tests.

steps.title: Choose cleanup by what changed

blocks.text: Know which runner your project actually uses

Jest and Vitest share many concepts and APIs, but configuration, environment setup, mocks, and globals can differ. This repository uses Vitest with React Testing Library, so new examples should follow its configured test environment and imports. Do not add Jest merely because a course mentions it; first understand the existing runner, scripts, and setup. Tests should run locally and in CI with the same intended configuration.

blocks.title: Keep tests deterministic and independent
blocks.text: Control clocks, random values, API responses, and global state when they affect an assertion. Clean up after tests and avoid depending on test order. A test should fail because the behavior changed—not because an external service was slow or a previous test left state behind.

blocks.text: Deep dive: test user-visible contracts and choose the right query

A useful UI test protects a behavior a user or another part of the app depends on, not the component's private implementation. Testing Library encourages queries that resemble how people find controls—role and accessible name first. Query choice communicates timing: `getBy` expects an immediate match, `queryBy` is useful to assert absence, and `findBy` waits for an asynchronous appearance. In this repository use its Vitest setup rather than copying Jest-only setup commands from older reference material.

steps.explanation: The heading appears only after the request completes, so findByRole waits for it. An immediate getByRole here would be timing-sensitive.

steps.explanation: queryBy returns null when no match exists, making it suitable for absence assertions. getBy would throw before the assertion could check absence.

blocks.title: An async UI test needs to await the condition, not sleep
blocks.text: Avoid fixed timeouts like `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000))` as a general solution. Wait for the expected element/state with the proper async query or waitFor, so the test is both faster and less timing-sensitive.
